Module 11.2›Chapter 11.2›Understanding Chaos Engineering
Core Concept

Understanding Chaos Engineering

Proactively Identifying Weaknesses in Distributed Systems

Intentional Failure Injection

Chaos Engineering is the disciplined practice of introducing failures into a system to observe its behavior and build confidence in its resilience. It's not about random destruction, but controlled experimentation.

  • •Moves beyond traditional testing of expected behaviors.
  • •Uncovers hidden vulnerabilities before they cause outages.
  • •Builds a stronger understanding of system dependencies.
Analogy Card

The System Vaccine

Imagine your system as a living organism. Chaos Engineering is like administering a vaccine: a small, controlled dose of a 'disease' (failure) to stimulate its immune system and build resilience against future, larger threats. This proactive approach strengthens the system's ability to recover.

Key Takeaway

Chaos Engineering transforms reactive incident response into proactive resilience building by systematically exposing and fixing weaknesses before they impact customers.

Common Mistake

Running experiments without a clear hypothesis or a defined 'steady state' can lead to uncontrolled outages instead of valuable insights.

screens.title: Hypothesize About Steady-State Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: The first and most crucial principle of Chaos Engineering, as pioneered by Netflix, is to hypothesize about steady-state behavior. Before you can intentionally break something, you must first understand what 'normal' looks like for your system. This involves defining measurable outputs that indicate the system is functioning correctly and delivering value to its users. For example, a steady-state hypothesis might be that your application maintains 99.9% uptime, or that its average response time remains consistently under 200 milliseconds, even during peak load. These metrics serve as your baseline. Without a clear definition of steady-state, you won't be able to accurately determine if your chaos experiment has caused a deviation or if the system has successfully maintained its expected behavior under stress. This foundational step ensures that your experiments are scientific and yield actionable insights, rather than just random observations. Module 11.2›Chapter 11.2›Steady-State Hypothesis
Core Principle 1

Hypothesize About Steady-State Behavior

Defining 'Normal' to Detect Anomalies

Establish a Baseline

Before injecting faults, define what 'normal' system operation looks like. This includes measurable outputs that indicate healthy performance and user experience.

  • •Examples: 99.9% uptime, average response time < 200ms.
  • •Serves as the control group for your experiment.
  • •Essential for determining if an experiment caused a deviation.
Example Scenario

E-commerce Checkout Service

For an e-commerce checkout service, a steady-state hypothesis might be: 'During peak hours, 99% of checkout transactions complete within 5 seconds, and the error rate remains below 0.1%.' This provides clear, quantifiable metrics to monitor during a chaos experiment.

Key Takeaway

Without a clear, measurable steady-state hypothesis, chaos experiments lack a meaningful baseline, making it difficult to interpret results and identify true weaknesses.

Common Misconception

Assuming 'no errors' means 'steady state'. A system might be slow or degraded without throwing explicit errors, still impacting user experience.

screens.title: Vary Real-World Events
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've established your steady-state hypothesis, the next principle is to vary real-world events. This means introducing failures that could realistically occur in your production environment, rather than just theoretical or edge-case scenarios. The goal is to simulate the types of disruptions that your system is most likely to encounter, such as sudden spikes in network latency, the unexpected crash of a server, or a critical resource becoming exhausted. For example, you might inject network delays between microservices, simulate high C P U pressure on a database server, or even temporarily disable a specific service instance. By exposing your system to these common, yet often unpredictable, real-world events, you can observe how it behaves under stress and identify vulnerabilities that might otherwise go unnoticed. This proactive approach helps your system build 'immunity' to these failures, much like a vaccine prepares the body for a virus, ensuring it can gracefully degrade or recover when actual incidents occur. Core Principle 2

Vary Real-World Events

Simulating Realistic Failures to Build Immunity

Inject Realistic Faults

Introduce events that mimic actual failures likely to occur in a production environment, such as network issues, resource exhaustion, or service outages.

  • •Network latency or packet loss.
  • •High CPU or memory pressure.
  • •Service crashes or dependency failures.
Example Faults

Common Failure Scenarios

  • •**Network Latency:** Simulate slow communication between microservices.
  • •**Resource Exhaustion:** Inject high CPU or memory usage on a VM.
  • •**Service Dependency Failure:** Temporarily disable a critical backend service.
  • •**Disk I/O Errors:** Simulate issues with storage access.
Key Takeaway

Focusing on realistic failure modes ensures that the resilience built through chaos experiments directly addresses the most probable threats to your system's stability.

screens.title: Run Experiments in Production
screens.narratorSegment: While it's prudent to begin chaos experiments in lower environments like staging or development, the third core principle emphasizes running experiments in production. This might sound counter-intuitive or even risky, but it's where the most valuable insights are gained. Production environments are unique; they have real user traffic, complex data patterns, and intricate dependencies that are often impossible to replicate perfectly in non-production settings. For example, a network latency experiment in a staging environment might show no impact, but in production, with thousands of concurrent users and external A P I calls, the same latency could expose a critical bottleneck or a cascading failure. By running experiments directly in production, albeit with extreme caution and safety measures, you can uncover true system behaviors and dependencies that only manifest under real-world conditions, ultimately building a much higher level of confidence in your system's resilience. Core Principle 3

Run Experiments in Production

Uncovering Real-World Dependencies and Behaviors

Real-World Insights

The most valuable insights come from experiments conducted in production environments, where real traffic, data, and dependencies exist.

  • •Non-production environments rarely replicate production complexity.
  • •Uncovers hidden dependencies and race conditions.
  • •Requires extreme caution and robust safety mechanisms.
Why Production Matters

Unique Production Characteristics

  • •**Real Traffic Patterns:** Actual user load and behavior.
  • •**Complex Data:** Live data sets and their interactions.
  • •**External Dependencies:** Integrations with third-party services.
  • •**Monitoring Fidelity:** Validation of actual alerting and observability.
Key Takeaway

While risky, production experiments provide unparalleled insights into system resilience, revealing vulnerabilities that only manifest under real-world conditions.

screens.title: Minimize Blast Radius & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: The fifth and arguably most critical principle is to minimize the blast radius and prioritize safety. When intentionally introducing failures, it's paramount to design experiments that affect the smallest possible segment of users or services. This limits the potential impact if something goes unexpectedly wrong. For example, you might target only a single instance of a microservice, or a specific region with low traffic, rather than an entire fleet. Crucially, every experiment must have a clear 'kill switch' or 'stop button' that allows you to immediately halt the experiment if it causes unintended or severe issues. This mechanism is your safety net, preventing a controlled experiment from escalating into an uncontrolled outage. Always start small, in non-critical parts of your system, and gradually increase the scope as you gain confidence. This principle ensures that while you're learning from failure, you're doing so responsibly and with minimal disruption to your customers.   • •Implement robust monitoring and alerting.

screens.title: Introducing Azure Chaos Studio
screens.narratorSegment: Now that we understand the core principles, let's explore how Azure helps you implement Chaos Engineering. Module 11.2›Chapter 11.2›Azure DevOps Pipeline
Code Walkthrough

Azure DevOps Pipeline for Chaos

Conceptual YAML for Automated Experimentation

Pipeline Stages

Key Steps in the YAML

  • •**`DeployToStaging`**: Standard application deployment.
  • •**`RunChaosExperiment`**: Orchestrates the chaos test.
  • •**`AzureCLI` Task**: Starts the Chaos Studio experiment.
  • •**`PowerShell` Task**: Monitors system health during the experiment.
  • •**`ManualValidation` Task**: Requires human approval to proceed.
Key Takeaway

This YAML demonstrates how to embed automated chaos experiments into your CI/CD, creating a robust validation gate that ensures resilience with every deployment.

stages:
- stage: DeployToStaging
  displayName: 'Deploy to Staging'
  jobs:
  - deployment: Deploy
    environment: 'Staging'
    pool:
      vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'
    strategy:
      runOnce:
        deploy:
          steps:
          - task: AzureRmWebAppDeployment@4
            displayName: 'Deploy App to Staging'
            inputs:
              azureSubscription: '$(azureServiceConnection)'
              WebAppName: 'mywebapp-staging'
              package: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop/app.zip'

- stage: RunChaosExperiment
  displayName: 'Run Chaos Experiment on Staging'
  dependsOn: DeployToStaging
  jobs:
  - job: RunChaos
    displayName: 'Execute Chaos Studio Experiment'
    pool:
      vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'
    steps:
    - task: AzureCLI@2
      displayName: 'Start Chaos Studio Experiment'
      inputs:
        azureSubscription: '$(azureServiceConnection)'
        scriptType: 'bash'
        scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
        inlineScript: |
          EXPERIMENT_NAME="HighCpuAppServiceExperiment"
          RESOURCE_GROUP="my-chaos-rg"
          echo "Starting Chaos Studio experiment: $EXPERIMENT_NAME"
          az chaos experiment start --name $EXPERIMENT_NAME --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP

    - task: PowerShell@2
      displayName: 'Monitor System During Experiment'
      inputs:
        targetType: 'inline'
        script: |
          Write-Host "Monitoring system for 10 minutes during chaos experiment..."
          Start-Sleep -Seconds 600 # Wait for the experiment duration + observation time
          $experimentStatus = az chaos experiment show --name $EXPERIMENT_NAME --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --query properties.status.executionStatus --output tsv
          if ($experimentStatus -ne "Completed") {
              Write-Error "Chaos experiment did not complete successfully or is still running."
              exit 1
          }

    - task: AzureCLI@2
      displayName: 'Stop Chaos Studio Experiment (if not auto-stopped)'
      condition: always() # Ensure this runs even if previous steps fail
      inputs:
        azureSubscription: '$(azureServiceConnection)'
        scriptType: 'bash'
        scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
        inlineScript: |
          EXPERIMENT_NAME="HighCpuAppServiceExperiment"
          RESOURCE_GROUP="my-chaos-rg"
          echo "Stopping Chaos Studio experiment: $EXPERIMENT_NAME"
          az chaos experiment cancel --name $EXPERIMENT_NAME --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP || true

    - task: ManualValidation@0
      displayName: 'Review Chaos Experiment Results'
      inputs:
        instructions: 'Review monitoring dashboards and logs for any unexpected behavior during the chaos experiment. Approve to proceed or reject to investigate/rollback.'

The first and most crucial principle of Chaos Engineering, as pioneered by Netflix, is to hypothesize about steady-state behavior. Before you can intentionally break something, you must first understand what 'normal' looks like for your system. This involves defining measurable outputs that indicate the system is functioning correctly and delivering value to its users. For example, a steady-state hypothesis might be that your application maintains 99.9% uptime, or that its average response time remains consistently under 200 milliseconds, even during peak load. These metrics serve as your baseline. Without a clear definition of steady-state, you won't be able to accurately determine if your chaos experiment has caused a deviation or if the system has successfully maintained its expected behavior under stress. This foundational step ensures that your experiments are scientific and yield actionable insights, rather than just random observations.
